\begin{abstract}
Continuous camera monitoring of captive marine animals produces far more video
than caretakers can review, yet most of it is used only reactively. We present
an automated vision--language pipeline that converts months of continuous
multi-camera aquarium footage of a single \emph{Octopus vulgaris} into a
quantified behavioural and affective-state time-series. The pipeline detects
when the animal is visible (a frozen CLIP encoder with a lightweight probe under
aspect-preserving preprocessing), extracts short behaviour clips gated on
visibility and motion, and re-prompts a large vision--language model to emit a
structured behavioural record per clip (behaviour class, posture, activity,
location, context and body colour). Aggregating $3{,}083$ analysed clips yields
an interpretable activity budget, an exposure-normalised circadian profile with a
late-afternoon activity peak, and a clear stimulus response in which human
presence nearly doubles movement and raises a transparent arousal index. To make
the system deployable and self-hosting, we distil the large teacher into small
local models: a captioning student (Qwen3-VL-2B~\cite{qwenvl}, QLoRA) that runs
4-bit on a laptop, and a single-class octopus mask model auto-labelled by
GroundingDINO and SAM2 and subsequently anchored by human-verified masks. On a
leak-free human-labelled test (122 frames from five held-out source videos) that
model reaches $0.64$ mean / $0.72$ median IoU with $1.1\%$ body-area error, and
the \emph{same} model separates present from empty frames at AUC $0.79$,
rejecting tank-glass reflections, a dominant false-positive source. On top of
the masks we extract an \emph{anatomical skeleton}---mantle, head and up to eight
arm splines---scored on a frozen benchmark by arm-tip F1 against protrusions of
the human mask ($0.54$; precision $0.72$, recall $0.50$), a metric we adopted
only after establishing that ``arms per frame'' is not a score and that the new
metric's own ground truth was itself wrong; its occlusion-honest arm kinematics
independently reproduce the ordering of the VLM-derived behaviour classes
(resting $63$ vs.\ reaching $159$\,px\,s$^{-1}$ arm-tip speed),
cross-validating both signals. We frame
results in terms of arousal and behavioural state rather than emotion, report
the pipeline's current limitations honestly---including several measured
negative results---and position the work as the profiling layer complementary
to real-time single-behaviour response systems.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Computer Vision; Vision--Language Models; Behaviour Analysis; Marine Animal
Welfare; Model Distillation; Edge AI; Cephalopods
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
Aquarium and controlled-habitat monitoring increasingly relies on
continuous camera coverage, but the resulting video vastly exceeds what human
caretakers can review. Most footage is therefore consulted only reactively,
after an event, and the rich record of an animal's day-to-day behaviour is left
unquantified. For welfare-oriented husbandry the more valuable question is
longitudinal: \emph{how does this animal spend its time, how does its rhythm
look, and how does it respond to its environment?}

Octopuses make this both important and hard. They are highly intelligent,
behaviourally complex invertebrates whose welfare is a growing concern, yet their
non-rigid bodies, rapid posture changes, active camouflage, frequent denning, and
the reflections and floating debris of tank environments defeat naive visual
monitoring~\cite{disc_o}. A companion line of work from our consortium targets a
single, actionable behaviour---a ``protest'' limb gesture used to request tank
lighting---and closes the loop by automatically actuating the lights. That system
is reactive and behaviour-specific by design.

This paper addresses the complementary problem: \emph{understanding the whole
behavioural repertoire over time}. We present an automated pipeline that turns
continuous multi-camera footage of one captive \emph{O.\ vulgaris} (``Nity'')
into a structured behavioural and affective-state time-series, together with the
small local models needed to run it cheaply and offline. Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item An end-to-end pipeline from raw footage to a per-clip \emph{structured
behavioural record}, using a large vision--language model (VLM) as a
zero-shot behavioural annotator with snap-to-list validation.
\item An aggregate behavioural analysis of the animal over several months: an
interpretable activity budget, an exposure-normalised circadian profile, and a
quantified stimulus response, framed as arousal / behavioural state.
\item Teacher$\rightarrow$student distillation into deployable local models---a
4-bit captioning student that runs on a laptop, and a single-class octopus
segmentation model auto-labelled by GroundingDINO$+$SAM2, anchored by
human-verified masks, and evaluated leak-free on a held-out human-labelled test
($0.64$ mean / $0.72$ median IoU, $1.1\%$ body-area error and presence
AUC $0.79$ --- all from one model on one test set); its mask-area signal
robustly rejects reflections.
\item An anatomical skeleton and kinematics layer on top of the masks:
per-frame mantle/head/arm graphs scored by arm-tip F1 on a frozen benchmark,
with the arm-selection gates reported as an explicit precision--recall frontier
rather than a single tuned point; occlusion-honest arm tracking; and per-arm
kinematics that independently reproduce the VLM behaviour ordering---a
cross-validation of two unrelated signal paths.
\item A frozen benchmark suite (segmentation, skeleton, tracking; one runner,
tagged results, video-level splits) and an honest account of methodology and
limitations around it, including measured negative results: a train--test
leakage we caught and corrected, a headline metric we had to retire because a
genuine improvement made it worse, a metric ground truth we had to validate and
fix, and several plausible improvements that failed under the fixed benchmark.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}
\textbf{Cephalopod behaviour and welfare.} Interest in octopus cognition and
welfare has grown alongside their inclusion in animal-welfare frameworks. Prior
consortium work introduced a framework for decoding inter-species communication
with octopodes and a real-time detector for a light-request behaviour that
actuates the habitat~\cite{disc_o}. Our work is the profiling counterpart to that
response system.

\textbf{Foundation models as annotators.} General-purpose VLMs can describe and
classify images zero-shot, and open-vocabulary detectors and promptable
segmenters (GroundingDINO~\cite{groundingdino}, SAM/SAM2~\cite{sam2}) enable
labelling without task-specific supervision. We use these as \emph{teachers}: an
expensive model produces structured labels that we distil into small
students~\cite{lora}. CLIP~\cite{clip} provides the frozen visual features for our
lightweight presence detector; the deployed segmenter uses an efficient
LR-ASPP/MobileNetV3 head~\cite{mobilenetv3}.

\section{System and Methods}
The tank is observed by a multi-camera rig (6 IP cameras, 4K, infrared and colour
night vision) with a manually selected region of interest around the den for each
camera; the same installation supports the companion response system. The
pipeline (Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}) has four stages.

\subsection{Visibility Detection}
A frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 encoder feeds a small multi-layer-perceptron probe
(512$\rightarrow$256$\rightarrow$64$\rightarrow$2) trained to classify
\emph{octopus-visible} vs.\ \emph{hidden}. The single most important design choice
was preprocessing: CLIP's default centre-crop discards $33$--$44\%$ of a 16:9
frame, and \emph{aspect-ratio mismatch}---not backbone capacity---was the root
cause of poor field performance. Replacing the crop with aspect-preserving
letterbox padding, and mining $\sim$1.7k reflection/infrared-noise hard
negatives, gave a probe that reaches $96.8\%$ on our internal detection test set
while sharply reducing confident false positives on reflections.

\subsection{Clip Extraction}
For each source video we compute, per second, the probe's visibility probability
and an absolute changed-pixel motion fraction (with the burned-in timestamp region
masked so the ticking clock is not counted as motion). A non-overlapping
$20\,\mathrm{s}$ window is kept when the octopus is visible for a majority of the
window and mean motion exceeds a threshold. We deliberately use the
\emph{absolute} changed-pixel fraction: per-video normalised motion incorrectly
promotes static scenes (e.g.\ a flickering lamp) to ``motion''.

\subsection{Structured Behavioural Extraction}
Rather than treating a caption as the end product, we treat it as one field of a
\emph{structured behavioural record}. For each extracted clip we select the
clearest frames (contrast-enhanced for the dim infrared footage, scored by the
visibility probe) and prompt a large VLM (Qwen3-VL-235B~\cite{qwenvl}, accessed
via API) to
return a JSON record: \{present, behaviour (7-class ethogram), posture, activity
level, location, context, body colour, colour/texture change, confidence\}. Each
field is validated by snapping to an allowed value list; colour fields are gated
per clip, so infrared/greyscale clips (detected by low BGR channel divergence) are
instructed to leave colour \emph{uncertain}. The run over $3{,}205$ clips cost
$\approx\$2.22$ ($\sim\$0.0006$/clip). We note---and exploit---that the VLM is a
far stronger presence filter than the detector: on one batch it judged $63\%$ of
detector-``verified'' clips to actually contain no octopus, almost all tank-glass
reflections.

\subsection{Distillation to Local Models}
\label{sec:distill}
A central design principle is that the expensive foundation models are used only
as \emph{offline teachers}; nothing large is deployed. Their outputs become
training data for small students, so the running system is self-hosting and
needs no GPU server or paid API. We apply the same teacher$\rightarrow$student
recipe twice: the VLM's captions distil into a compact captioning model, and the
GroundingDINO$+$SAM2 masks into a single-class segmentation model
(Sec.~\ref{sec:models}). The student is kept as small as the task allows---one
class, low input resolution---so continuous in-situ inference is feasible on
commodity hardware.

\subsection{Diverse-Footage Harvesting}
\label{sec:harvest}
Early models were trained on footage from a single week, which we found to be
the binding generalisation limit. We therefore built a streaming harvester that
crawls the archive and, for each candidate video, \emph{probes} a handful of
frames before committing to a full scan---skipping empty ``den'' videos cheaply.
Because the server imposes a low aggregate bandwidth cap (measured
$\sim$5\,MB/s, parallel connections yielding only $1.6\times$), it runs as a
single CPU worker that streams rather than bulk-downloads, keeping short clips
and a coverage ledger so skipped footage can be revisited. This expanded
coverage from $7$ days to $>\!100$ distinct days.

\subsection{Evaluation Protocol: a Frozen Benchmark Suite}
\label{sec:bench}
A pipeline this long makes it easy to accumulate numbers each measured on a
slightly different set. We therefore froze three benchmarks behind a single
runner writing tagged results, so that every improvement claim here is a
before/after on the same data. \emph{SEG-TEST}: $122$ human-labelled mask frames
plus $19$ empty-mask negatives, from five source videos excluded from
\emph{every} training source; mask IoU, body-area error, presence AUC.
\emph{SKEL-50}: $50$ frozen frames over $20$ source videos, each with image,
human mask and model mask; arm-tip F1. \emph{TRACK-10}: $10$ frozen clips
spanning all six behaviour classes, three cameras and three dates; teleport
rate, occluded fraction, coverage. Two rules hold throughout: splits are by
\emph{source video}, never by frame---frames from one recording are
near-duplicates and we shipped that bug once (Sec.~\ref{sec:models})---and the
frozen lists are never regenerated to suit a result
(Table~\ref{tab:benchmarks}).

\section{Behavioural and Affective-State Analysis}
Aggregating the $3{,}083$ present clips (joined to absolute clock time) yields an
interpretable behavioural profile. We stress a framing choice: we report
\textbf{arousal and behavioural state}, not emotion. Our transparent arousal index
is $0.6\cdot\mathrm{activity} + 0.4\cdot\mathrm{posture\text{-}spread}$, with
static body colour as a secondary channel available only on colour cameras.

% FIGURE: activity budget + circadian + stimulus-response (from data/behaviour_dashboard.html)
\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.48\textwidth]{assets/behaviour_findings.pdf}
    \caption{Aggregate behaviour: (a) activity budget; (b) exposure-normalised
    circadian visible-activity rate; (c) motion and arousal with vs.\ without human
    presence. Generated from the structured records.}
    \label{fig:findings}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Activity budget.} Exploration/manipulation $41\%$, resting $33\%$,
human/enrichment interaction $14\%$, reaching out of water $9\%$, crawling $2\%$,
swimming/jetting $1\%$.

\textbf{Circadian structure.} Normalising present-clip counts by all extracted
windows per hour (an exposure correction) reveals a strong diel pattern: visible
activity is $\sim$1--5\% overnight, rises to a $\sim$45\% peak at 17:00 with a
13:00--19:00 plateau, plus a dawn bump around 05:00--06:00.

\textbf{Stimulus response.} Comparing clips with vs.\ without a human present, mean
motion nearly doubles ($0.045\rightarrow0.095$) and the arousal index rises
($0.46\rightarrow0.68$). On colour cameras, the dark red-brown body colour is most
common at baseline ($\sim$16\%) and less so during human interaction ($\sim$6\%),
consistent with a colour/posture shift under stimulus.

We regard the \emph{contrasts} (e.g.\ human-present vs.\ absent) as the robust
findings; absolute levels depend on the upstream presence gate and will shift as
the detector improves.

\section{Local Models}
\label{sec:models}
\subsection{Captioning Student}
We distil the teacher's one-sentence descriptions into Qwen3-VL-2B~\cite{qwenvl}
using QLoRA (rank 16). On a $50$-clip held-out split, embedding similarity to the teacher
improves from $0.702$ (base model) to $0.834$ and ROUGE-L from $0.269$ to
$0.455$. Merged and quantised to 4-bit with MLX, the student is $\sim$1.7\,GB and
produces a caption in $\sim$3\,s on a 16\,GB laptop with no GPU; a cross-platform
Transformers backend covers non-Apple hardware.

\subsection{Segmentation Student}
Following the distillation principle of Sec.~\ref{sec:distill}, we target the
\emph{smallest} model that yields usable masks: a single foreground class at low
resolution, with GroundingDINO$+$SAM2 acting purely as an offline auto-labeller,
never deployed. To obtain masks without hand labelling, the teacher pairs
GroundingDINO (box) with SAM2 (mask): the most-confident frame seeds SAM2 video
propagation, and largest-blob plus area-continuity cleanup remove transient
errors. This corrected the two systematic failures of per-frame prompting
(infrared bright-tool bleed, colour background bleed) and, importantly, rejects the
reflection camera by low seed confidence. Auto-labelling produced $4{,}412$
(image, mask) pairs, from which we distilled candidate students spanning a
size sweep (a compact U-Net at several widths and an LR-ASPP head); we retain the
smallest model clearing our quality bar, an LR-ASPP student of $3.2$\,M
parameters.

Used as a \emph{presence} signal, the mask area is reflection-robust, directly
attacking the pipeline's dominant false-positive source; training with
empty-mask negatives is what makes this work, as a positives-only student was a
coin flip (AUC $0.50$). On SEG-TEST the deployed model reaches presence AUC
$0.794$ ($122$ present vs.\ $19$ empty frames)---the same model and test set as
the IoU reported below, so the two describe one system. An earlier
negatives-trained variant, evaluated separately against a reflection-heavy set
from the tank-glass camera, reached AUC $0.86$ overall and $0.99$ against
reflections with $0\%$ reflection false-positives at area $0.01$ and $88\%$
present-recall; that is a different model on a different set, and we do not
merge the two figures.

\textbf{Raising mask quality: what worked and what did not.} Early students
plateaued near $0.47$ IoU across model sizes, architectures and augmentation. We
resolved this through a sequence of controlled experiments, each evaluated on
fixed splits, and report the failures alongside the successes because they
changed our conclusions. (i)~\emph{Video diversity} (expanding training from $62$
to $176$ distinct source videos via the harvest of Sec.~\ref{sec:harvest})
helped modestly and robustly ($0.468\!\rightarrow\!0.494$ on a harder,
diverse-date validation). (ii)~\emph{Cleaner teacher labels did not help}:
re-labelling everything with larger teacher models (GroundingDINO-base,
SAM2-large) left held-out IoU flat ($0.494\!\rightarrow\!0.506$); an earlier
signal suggesting label noise was the ceiling turned out to be
\emph{train--test leakage}---two label sources shared source videos---which we
caught, corrected with a hard video-level holdout, and re-measured.
(iii)~\emph{Human-verified masks}: a click-to-SAM2 labelling tool (one click
seeds SAM2, the human corrects) produced $412$ positive and $87$ empty-mask
human labels; training on human labels alone underperformed the blend ($0.505$
vs.\ $0.608$)---at this scale, label volume beats purity---but they provide the
project's first \emph{human-verified held-out test set}. (iv)~The decisive
levers were found by inspecting failures on that test set: the octopus occupies
a median $2.5\%$ of the frame, so at the original $256^2$ input its arms are
$1$--$2$ pixels wide---unrepresentable; and the symmetric Dice$+$BCE loss did
not penalise under-segmentation. Training at $512^2$ with a focal Tversky loss
($\beta\!>\!\alpha$, penalising false negatives) on human$+$teacher labels
yields $0.608$ mean / $0.666$ median IoU on the leak-free human-verified test,
up from a $0.466$ baseline; pushing the input to $768^2$ with $\beta{=}0.8$,
which chiefly improves thin-structure recall, gives the model we deploy:
\textbf{$0.642$ mean / $0.719$ median IoU} with $1.05\%$ body-area error on the
same $122$-frame test (Table~\ref{tab:benchmarks}). It also dominates the
$512^2$ variant on presence ($0.794$ vs.\ $0.718$ AUC), so the same checkpoint
serves both the presence gate and the skeleton extraction of
Sec.~\ref{sec:skeleton}. We note the residual IoU gap is dominated by thin arm
boundaries; the \emph{area} signal that the behavioural analysis consumes
(posture spread, presence) is accurate to $\sim\!1\%$.

\section{Anatomical Skeleton and Arm Kinematics}
\label{sec:skeleton}
The masks enable a further, more structured representation: a per-frame
\emph{anatomical skeleton}---a mantle centre, a head node, and up to eight arm
splines with base/mid/tip landmarks---from which per-arm kinematics (tip speed,
posture spread) are derived. Extraction is classical: topology-preserving
thinning of the silhouette, Dijkstra arm-path selection from an anatomical root,
and mask-constrained splines.

\textbf{A frozen benchmark and measured fixes.} All skeleton work is evaluated
on SKEL-50 (Sec.~\ref{sec:bench}): $50$ frozen frames, each with image,
human-verified mask and model mask. The headline metric is \emph{arm-tip F1}
against the protrusions of the \emph{human} mask, matched greedily one-to-one
within $5\%$ of the image diagonal, so that a duplicate arm cannot match the
same protrusion twice and both missed and spurious arms are penalised.
Decomposing the loss per stage (silhouette $\rightarrow$ thinning $\rightarrow$
selection) located the errors and produced the fixes we ship: relaxed
arm-selection floors that had discarded genuinely short, curled arms; mask
preparation whose blur threshold erased thin arms; an anatomically constrained
head; the higher-resolution segmentation student of Sec.~\ref{sec:models}; and,
for offline analysis, SAM2 refinement of the student's mask (the student
\emph{locates}, SAM2 \emph{sharpens}). The head rule replaced a
widest-second-blob heuristic that placed the head plausibly in only $9\%$ of
frames by a neck-constriction rule between mantle and arm crown, which reached
$96\%$ when it was introduced and reads $80\%$ under the current, stricter
arm-selection gates; that ``plausible'' criterion is loose---the head need only
lie between mantle and crown---and we are replacing it with pixel error against
human clicks on the eyes. Two plausible improvements measured as nulls and are
reported as such: skeletonising the segmentation \emph{probability field} with
hysteresis (the missing arms are not sub-threshold---the student genuinely does
not see them), and a zoom-in second segmentation pass (crops are
out-of-distribution for the student). For context on the ceiling, running the
same protrusion detector on the \emph{human} masks yields a mean of $5.7$
(median $6$, maximum $8$) arm protrusions per frame: a 2-D silhouette does not
expose arms folded under the body or foreshortened toward the camera, so even
perfect recall on this benchmark is recall against a subset of the animal's
eight arms.

\textbf{Choosing an operating point, not a number.} Arm selection carries two
``anti-mess'' gates---a unique-suffix requirement (an arm's unshared portion
must exceed a multiple of its root radius and a fraction of its length) and a
tip-thinness requirement---added after inspection showed duplicate late-forking
arms and stubs ending inside the body. On the benchmark these are a straight
precision-for-recall trade, so we report the whole frontier
(Table~\ref{tab:skel}) rather than only the shipped point: gates off maximises
F1 ($0.565$) but restores the tangle, our first setting was over-strict
($0.520$ at recall $0.468$), and the shipped setting sits between them
($0.539$, no measurable duplicates). We keep it because downstream kinematics
consume arm \emph{identities} over time, where a duplicated arm is worse than a
missing one---a design choice whose cost the table makes explicit.

\textbf{Two lessons about metrics.} Both came from this benchmark and both
changed what we report. First, \emph{arm count is not a score}: when the
anti-mess gates removed roughly $1.3$ duplicate or tangled arms per frame---a
visibly cleaner output---the count we had been tracking fell
$4.80\rightarrow3.48$, a $27\%$ ``regression'' produced by a genuine
improvement. Precision alone is equally gameable (emit one obvious arm), hence
F1 against human-mask protrusions, with arm count kept only as a descriptive
statistic. Second, \emph{the replacement metric's own ground truth was wrong}:
at its default sensitivity our protrusion detector counted contour bumps as
separate arms---mean $9.7$, up to $14$ per human mask---so the eight-arm cap
bound in $80\%$ of frames and recall was scored against partly fictional arms.
Requiring peaks to be $\geq\!10\%$ of the contour apart (closer peaks belong to
the same arm) moved the shipped configuration's tip-F1 from $0.441$ to $0.539$
(precision $0.685\!\rightarrow\!0.722$, recall $0.380\!\rightarrow\!0.502$).
Since the error was concentrated in recall, every pre-fix recall and F1 figure
is incomparable with the post-fix ones and any ranking built on the old ground
truth had to be re-measured; Table~\ref{tab:skel} is that re-measurement. The
generalisable lesson: validate a new metric's \emph{own} ground truth before
trusting any ranking it produces.

\begin{figure*}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.80\textwidth]{assets/skeleton_example.pdf}
    \caption{Qualitative example from the frozen benchmark (arm splines coloured,

\textbf{Occlusion-honest tracking and kinematics.} Across a clip, per-frame
skeletons are linked by seeding from the best-resolved frame and propagating
bidirectionally (median arms maintained across a clip rise from $2.2$ to
$5.8$), with a per-node optical-flow motion prior. Critically, every node
carries a state---\emph{detected}, \emph{fitted}, or \emph{occluded}---and
motion is computed \emph{only} from evidence-backed samples: instrumenting this
revealed that $42\%$ of arm samples in naive tracking were evidence-free holds
whose apparent smoothness masked fabricated stillness. A global
tracklet-association alternative measured worse than the gated chain and is
reported as a negative.

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.44\textwidth]{assets/kinematics_by_behaviour.pdf}
    \caption{State-gated arm-tip speed grouped by the VLM-assigned behaviour
    class (medians labelled). The two signals are computed by unrelated paths
    (geometry vs.\ language model), yet the kinematics reproduce the expected
    ordering.}
    \label{fig:kinematics}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Cross-validation of the two signal paths.} Merging per-clip kinematics
into the structured records gives an independent check on the VLM labels:
state-gated arm-tip speed orders the behaviour classes exactly as ethology
expects---resting $63$, crawling $101$, human interaction $136$,
exploration/manipulation $139$, reaching out of water $159$\,px\,s$^{-1}$
(Fig.~\ref{fig:kinematics})---with resting under half of the active classes.
Because the kinematic and language-model pathways share no components beyond
the raw video, their agreement is evidence that both measure real behaviour
rather than each other's artefacts. This is currently a consistency check, not a
statistical result: the medians are over $n{=}40$ clips, with the smallest
classes very thin (crawling $n{=}2$, resting $n{=}4$), and we report no
significance test. Kinematics are also reported in pixel units
(camera-relative); metric calibration is future work.

\section{Relevance to the OCEANS Community}
The work targets intelligent sensing and longitudinal behavioural analysis for
controlled marine habitats, aligning with OCEANS themes in imaging and vision
systems and in welfare-oriented monitoring, and it emphasises \emph{edge
deployability}: the distilled students run offline on commodity hardware,
avoiding cloud dependence for continuous in-situ monitoring. Where the companion
system acts on a single behaviour in real time, this pipeline supplies the
quantitative baseline against which such events---and future welfare
interventions---can be interpreted.

\section{Limitations and Ongoing Work}
We are deliberate about what is not yet established.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{Human-verified test sets exist only for segmentation.}
Segmentation now reports on a leak-free human-labelled held-out test
($499$ human masks; five source videos excluded from \emph{all} training
sources); detection and captioning numbers remain on internal splits, so we
make no comparative claims for those components yet.
\item \textbf{The VLM behaviour labels themselves are not yet validated.} Every
aggregate result is grouped by labels the structured extractor produced, and
their reliability is unmeasured; a frozen $250$-clip re-annotation benchmark
(stratified over behaviours, cameras and not-present clips, with a disjoint
frame sample to expose frame-selection sensitivity) is implemented but currently
blocked on an expired API credential. It measures the extractor's
\emph{consistency}, not its accuracy against a human ethologist, which remains
the larger open item.
\item \textbf{Leakage is easy and we hit it once.} Two label sources sharing
source videos silently placed test videos in training; an apparent
$0.49\!\rightarrow\!0.70$ improvement evaporated under a hard video-level
holdout. All segmentation and skeleton results reported here post-date that
correction; we recommend video-level holdouts as standard practice for
camera-trap-style data.
\item \textbf{Presence-gate noise propagates.} Absolute behavioural rates depend on
the detector; we report contrasts, which are robust to a constant gate bias.
\item \textbf{Context label is coarse.} The ``enrichment interaction'' context
fires whenever a permanent tank object is visible ($\sim$66\% of clips); the clean
stimulus contrast is human-present vs.\ absent.
\item \textbf{Skeleton and kinematics.} Arm recovery is silhouette-limited: even
human masks expose only $5.7$ arm protrusions per frame on average, and the
model's masks cost more, so tip recall stands at $0.50$; kinematics are in pixel
units without metric calibration and rest on $n{=}40$ clips;
infrared cameras are not yet covered by the colour-trained segmenter. A
static-feature behaviour classifier failed (below the majority baseline),
confirming that behaviour classification needs temporal/motion features rather
than more labels---which is what the kinematics layer supplies.
\end{itemize}
Ongoing work follows three tracks: scaling the state-gated kinematics from the
current subset to the full corpus, with video-level statistics, so per-behaviour
profiles reach statistical strength; distilling the structured behavioural
extractor into the local $2$-B student (JSON targets in place of a sentence);
and, to pass the silhouette ceiling, a learned keypoint model on RGB appearance
rather than masks, bootstrapped from the current skeleton outputs.

\section{Conclusion}
We presented an automated vision--language pipeline that converts continuous
octopus footage into a quantified behavioural and affective-state time-series, and
distils its large teachers into local models that run offline. The aggregate
analysis surfaces an interpretable activity budget, a clear circadian rhythm and a
measurable stimulus response; the segmentation student---evaluated leak-free on a
human-verified test---supplies a reflection-robust presence signal and the masks
for an anatomical skeleton whose occlusion-honest arm kinematics independently
reproduce the ordering of the language-model behaviour labels. Framed as arousal
and behavioural state, and reported together with the negative results and the
leakage lesson that shaped it, the system offers a practical, welfare-oriented
layer for longitudinal behavioural understanding in controlled marine habitats.

\section*{Ethical Statement and Data Availability}
The work was conducted in a private aquarium, with only sub-threshold interactions
w.r.t.\ EC directive 2010/63/EU of several caretakers with a single
\emph{O.\ vulgaris} (supplier: Flying Sharks, Portugal). Husbandry and enrichment
practices followed best practices for octopus aquariums in compliance with FELASA
guidelines. The video data used in the study are available from the last author.
